transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE); Priya Patel (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (Redwood SE); Rachel Owens (Head of ML, Cedar Ridge); Tom Alvarez (Platform Eng); Lina Park (Security); Ethan Moore (CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery to map Cedar Ridge's reserved GPU needs, isolation/topology requirements, burst/hotpool strategy, and KMS/HSM constraints for a potential Dedicated + Private deployment. Agreement to run a short benchmark and share security artifacts.

Topics discussed:
- Current infra and model types (7B open models + in-house fine-tuned 13B experiments)
- Expected steady state and peak QPS, burst patterns and pre-warm requirements
- Tenant isolation, VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM for key custody, audit logs
- Fallback plan: graceful degrade to hosted variants and canary policies
- Cost/latency tradeoffs (quantization, batching, KV cache)

Transcript (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Michael: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to run through your expected capacity needs and especially the isolation angle and K M S constraints. Rachel do you want to kick off with a little context on what you're running today?
[00:22] Rachel: Yeah sure, thanks Michael. So Cedar Ridge is building a physician-assist product, it annotates clinical notes and drafts suggestions. We have a steady background of synchronous requests from the web UI which is low QPS but tight p50 latency target of sub 250ms, and then big batched jobs overnight. We're running a mix of open-source 7B models in prod and experimenting with a fine-tuned 13B for higher quality.
[00:45] Tom: To add, our current infra is a mix of cloud VMs and an internal GPU cluster. We're constrained on ops headcount so we like Redwood because of managed serving, but security/keys are a hard P0 for us.
[01:03] Priya: Understood. When you say sub-250ms P50, is that for single-turn generation with roughly 32 tokens typical output? Also curious about your sequence length distribution for long notes.
[01:16] Rachel: Most UI replies are 20-60 tokens, yes. But clinicians sometimes paste long context windows up to 2k tokens; those are batched and offloaded to async workers.
[01:31] Michael: That helps. Our Dedicated offering would let you reserve a set of GPU nodes. We also offer an optional hotpool — pre-warmed instances that can absorb bursts. Typical questions folks have: how isolated do you need tenants to be, do you require customer-managed VPCs or on-prem private control planes, and what's your key custody requirement for encryption at rest?
[01:52] Lina: For keys we need strict control, ideally keys in our HSM, so Redwood would need to support external KMS/HSM integration or provide a hybrid where we manage keys. SOC2 + audit logs are required, also SSO/SAML with SCIM provisioning.
[02:08] Jordan: We do have KMS integrations, and for Private deployments customers can bring their own key manager through our KMS proxy and HSM connectors. There are two common patterns: we can route decryption requests through the private control plane so Redwood never sees plaintext keys, or for on-prem we can deploy the inference runtime behind your network and have direct HSM calls.
[02:33] Lina: When you say 'route through the control plane' can you clarify — does Redwood ever hold decrypted model artifacts, or are those always encrypted at rest?
[02:41] Priya: Good question. Models and checkpoints are encrypted at rest. For hosted Dedicated we encrypt model weights and decrypt on node at runtime; with a customer-managed KMS the decryption call is authorized by your tenant's key and recorded in audit logs. In Private/on-prem modes we can avoid cross-tenant access entirely and use local HSM calls.
[03:00] Tom: How about the fallback plan if the Dedicated pool is saturated — do you offer a graceful degrade to a hosted variant or a smaller quantized model? We need continuity for clinician UI.
[03:10] Michael: Yes we have smart routing policies. Typical pattern is primary serve on Dedicated nodes with a policy that will fallback to a compatible hosted model family or a quantized variant in the same latency band. You can configure canary and A/B rollout policies and automatic fallback thresholds. We also support circuit-breaker style rate-limiting to keep UI latency within bounds.
[03:34] Rachel: What's the cold start behavior for the hotpool? If we pre-warm a hotpool to handle morning surges, do nodes evict KV caches after idling, and what's the warmup time?
[03:45] Priya: Hotpool nodes keep model in GPU memory and maintain KV cache for active sessions. Warmup time depends on model size and topology; a 7B quantized model usually preloads in ~30-60s, 13B is more like 90-180s depending on GPU type. We offer a 'keep-alive' policy to avoid KV eviction for high priority tenants, but that consumes reserved memory/resources.
[04:07] Ethan: On GPUs, what hardware are you recommending for us — A100, H100, or say L4 for the smaller models? We want best cost vs latency tradeoff.
[04:17] Jordan: For 7B we often recommend L4 or A10g-like shapes for cost efficiency; for the 13B fine-tuned models H100 or A100 80GB is usually better to hit your sub-250ms P50 for shorter sequences if you need single-token latency. But quantization and kernel choices change that. We'll propose a mixed pool: L4-class for background and less latency-critical traffic, and one or two H100s for high-SLA endpoints.
[04:40] Tom: Is hybrid pooling supported — like routing small requests to warm L4s and escalating large requests to H100s? We need predictable tail latency.
[04:48] Priya: Absolutely — routing policy can be based on request labels, token budget, or model family. We also support burst policies: a reserved pool with a configured 'burst wallet' for short-term extra capacity. Burst capacity can either be from spare nodes in your Dedicated cluster (if available) or fallback to Redwood-hosted burst capacity if you allow it.
[05:08] Lina: We have a compliance constraint: patient data cannot leave our VPC for decryption or logging. Can Redwood run in a customer VPC/private control plane so logs and decrypts stay inside?
[05:19] Michael: Yes, Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane where logs are forwarded to your SIEM, and we can configure audit logging with minimal retention in Redwood's control plane if required. For strict data residency we can run everything in your VPC or even an on-prem package.
[05:35] Rachel: How does billing work for reserved nodes vs burst? Is burst billed at a higher rate?
[05:41] Michael: Typically reserved capacity is a fixed monthly commit and burst is usage-based premium (higher per-minute rate). We can model a blended rate for your expected pattern; we should run numbers on your token distribution.
[05:55] Tom: Ok, next on the ops side: what observability is exposed — token-level cost breakdown, trace for request path, and per-tenant latency histograms?
[06:03] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route latency histograms, token breakdown by prompt/output, tracing hooks, and a per-tenant cost dashboard. For Private deployments those dashboards can be shipped to your internal Grafana via our remote exporter.
[06:19] Rachel: Can we run a short benchmark? We'll want to test our 7B and the 13B finetuned to validate tail latency and KV cache behavior with our token profiles.
[06:27] Priya: Absolutely. Proposed plan: we run a 2-hour benchmark against a staging Dedicated pool with a small set of reserved nodes and hotpool enabled. We'll instrument KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, p50/p95, and cost per token. We'll need your model artifact and test harness or alternatively use a local copy of your tuned model behind an NDA.
[06:44] Michael: I'll send the security pack and NDA template. Lina, any other compliance questions up front?
[06:50] Lina: We need details on key rotation, KMS ACLs, and evidence of SOC2 audits. Also retention controls for logs and model prompts — clinicians' PHI must be redacted or never logged by default.
[07:03] Jordan: We have redaction modes and can configure prompt scrubbing. Audit logs and key rotation are supported; we can provide the SOC2 report and the KMS design doc.
[07:12] Tom: A couple of nitty-gritty questions: does Redwood support model sharding across GPUs for the 13B, or do you run single-node models? We sometimes need to split large models.
[07:21] Priya: We support both. For 13B many customers run single-GPU if they can use an 80GB GPU with quantization; otherwise we support tensor or pipeline parallelism with our runtime. Sharding impacts KV cache semantics a bit, so we'll capture that in the benchmark.
[07:36] Rachel: Latency SLA — can you do 99th percentile targets for UI? We know 99 is hard for gen models but it's critical for clinician experience.
[07:44] Michael: We offer SLA tiers tied to Dedicated. 99th percentile SLAs are available with higher reservation levels and prewarm guarantees. We can scope an SLA that maps to your p99 requirement once we know the pool sizing and traffic shape.
[07:58] Ethan: For fallback, if the Dedicated pool goes into emergency overload and you route to Hosted, what changes in terms of data handling and key custody?
[08:08] Priya: If you allow hosted fallback, we recommend one of two patterns: (1) host a quantized model in Redwood-hosted but route only non-PHI or redacted content there, or (2) if you need full PHI protection, we only fallback to other nodes inside your private control plane. Fallback to fully hosted endpoints would require you to allow key escrow to Redwood for that fallback path, which based on your compliance comments is unlikely.
[08:33] Lina: So hosted fallback is a non-starter for us unless we can guarantee no PHI is sent — ok.
[08:38] Michael: Understood. We'll plan to keep fallback within customer-managed resources.
[08:42] Rachel: What about encryption in transit and at rest? We need TLS mutual auth and disk-level encryption.
[08:49] Jordan: TLS 1.2+ mutual auth is supported for Private flows, and disk encryption is a given with encryption keys in your KMS.
[08:56] Tom: Can we talk about the operational runbook? For example, morning surge at 8am where we see a 7x spike for 5-8 minutes — do we need to size the reserved pool for that or rely on a hotpool + burst wallet?
[09:07] Priya: For short spikes, hotpool + burst wallet is usually ideal. Reserved nodes cover baseline, hotpool covers quick starts while burst wallet lets you spin additional nodes quickly. If spikes are predictable and frequent, you may prefer to reserve a larger pool to lower unit costs. We should model both scenarios against your historical traffic.
[09:25] Michael: Action item for Tom to share token distribution and a sample day with timestamps. That will let us calculate burn rates and propose a blended pricing.
[09:34] Tom: I'll send that.
[09:36] Rachel: A question on telemetry: can we mute logs entirely for certain endpoints (e.g., PHI routes)? We want minimal retention on Redwood's side.
[09:45] Priya: Yes, in Private mode you can configure log redaction and retention rules; you can also forward raw logs to your SIEM and keep only operational metrics in Redwood.
[09:54] Ethan: On the billing contract, are minimum terms 12 months for Dedicated?
[09:58] Michael: Standard reserved capacity has 12-month or 36-month commitments. We can discuss shorter pilots on a month-to-month reserved pilot but pricing will be at a higher effective committed rate.
[10:11] Rachel: Let's go through a concrete small pilot: 4 L4-class GPUs reserved for baseline, a hotpool of 2 nodes, and a 2-node H100 headroom for low-latency critical traffic. Can you model that?
[10:23] Michael: Yes, we'll run a cost/latency model and include a burst scenario where the hotpool can scale to 6 nodes for 10 minutes.
[10:30] Priya: For the benchmark we'll need your 7B and the 13B artifacts or access to a containerized inference server. Also need sample prompts and a token-length histogram.
[10:40] Rachel: We'll prepare that. One other quick point: we may want per-route RBAC so product and research teams have different quotas.
[10:47] Jordan: That's available—per-route RBAC and quotas are supported in Console and can be enforced at the control plane.
[10:54] Tom: Any known perf regressions with quantization for our type of clinical prompts? We care about hallucination risk.
[11:01] Priya: Quantization can slightly change outputs; we recommend running quality checks in the benchmark. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization/configs that minimize quality loss for your prompt set. We'll set up evals that measure F1/ROUGE-like metrics relevant to your use.
[11:18] Michael: Ok let's recap next steps — Michael to send SOC2 + KMS docs and NDA, Priya to schedule benchmark and prepare a harness, Tom to share traffic and token distributions, Lina to list compliance blockers if any, and Redwood to produce a preliminary pricing and pool sizing doc.
[11:36] Rachel: That works. Anything else?
[11:40] Michael: Nope, appreciate the time. We'll get the docs over by Friday.
[11:44] Tom: Thanks all.
[11:46] Meeting end.
